identity.title: Decentralized Attention Fails Centralized Signals: Rethinking Transformers for Medical Time Series

problem.claim: Analyze medical time-series signals containing both within-channel temporal dependencies and cross-channel dependencies.

gap.claim: Transformer-based models often capture temporal dependencies but struggle with channel dependencies because decentralized attention mismatches the centralized structure of medical signals.

contributions.claim: CoTAR, a centralized MLP-based module, replaces decentralized attention with a global core token that mediates token interaction through centralized aggregation and redistribution.
The proposed design is intended to align with centralized medical signals while reducing computational complexity from quadratic to linear.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish CoTAR by using a global core-token aggregation-redistribution mechanism as a centralized alternative to direct all-token attention.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments on five benchmarks showing superiority in effectiveness and efficiency.
On APAVA, the authors report up to a 12.13% improvement, with 33% memory usage and 20% inference time relative to the previous state of the art.
The authors report that code and all training scripts are available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Medical time-series analysis is presented as relevant to diagnosing brain and heart diseases.
The abstract identifies temporal dependencies within channels and channel dependencies across channels.
Transformers are described as effective for temporal modeling but weaker on channel dependencies because decentralized attention mismatches centralized signals.
CoTAR uses a global core token to centralize inter-token aggregation and redistribution, with linear rather than quadratic complexity.
The authors report gains across five benchmarks, including APAVA improvement and reduced memory and inference time.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly connects a signal's centralized structure to a replacement for decentralized attention, rather than presenting the module independently of the data geometry.

lessons.interpretation: Matching an architecture's interaction pattern to the dominant structure of the data can make the design rationale more explanatory.
lessons.application: When proposing a sequence model, state the data's dependency geometry, identify the mismatch in the baseline interaction mechanism, and make the replacement mechanism directly address that mismatch.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the data genuinely requires unconstrained pairwise interactions or when centralization discards important localized relationships.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the five benchmarks, task metrics, baselines, statistical variability, or experimental settings.
The reported APAVA improvement and resource ratios lack metric definitions and normalization details; the abstract does not establish independent validity or reproducibility.
